questions.q: Why does the lesson say a 150-case eval dataset needs automated grading?
options: Because a dataset is only useful if something can grade all the cases consistently and fast enough to run on every change, without a human reading every response
Because automated grading is required by law
Because eval datasets expire after 24 hours
Because human reviewers are not allowed to read AI output
questions.explain: The lesson explains automated metrics exist so a full dataset can be graded consistently on every prompt or model change, not read manually each time.

questions.q: What is 'LLM-as-judge' (model-graded) evaluation, per the lesson?
options: A legal process for AI-related disputes
A second model reading the output against a written rubric and returning a pass/fail with a reason
A method for training a model from scratch
A technique for compressing model weights
questions.explain: The lesson describes LLM-as-judge as using a second model to grade output against a rubric, making open-ended text practical to grade at scale.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does 'faithfulness' (or groundedness) specifically measure for a RAG system?
options: How fast the model responds
Whether the answer sticks to what the retrieved source documents actually say, rather than adding unsupported claims
How much the API costs per request
Whether the user liked the response emotionally
questions.explain: The lesson defines faithfulness/groundedness as whether a RAG answer stays consistent with what the retrieved sources actually say.

questions.q: What limitation of exact/string match does the lesson point out?
options: It only works when there's essentially one acceptable phrasing of a correct answer, which is rare beyond short factual answers
It cannot be automated at all
It is slower than LLM-as-judge grading
It requires a GPU to run
questions.explain: The lesson notes exact match is fast and unambiguous but limited to cases with one acceptable phrasing.

questions.q: Per the lesson, what do aggregate charts (pass rate, score distribution, head-to-head comparison) add beyond a per-case results table?
options: They replace the need for an eval dataset entirely
They make a large eval run readable in seconds instead of requiring a full manual review of every case
They automatically fix any failing test cases
They are purely decorative and add no functional value
questions.explain: The lesson states aggregate views are what make a large run readable quickly, rather than requiring a case-by-case manual review.
